chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid and Al-Husayn ibn Saeed together, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Al-Husayn ibn Abdullah, from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Amr, from Ibn al-Hurr, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) during the days he came to Iraq, so he said to me: 'Enter upon Ismail ibn Ja'far, for he is ill; look at what his ailment is and describe to me something of the pain he feels.' He said: 'So I rose from his presence and entered upon Ismail, and I asked him about the pain he feels. He informed me of it, and a cure was prescribed for him in which was Nabidh. So he (Ismail) said: 'Nabidh is Haram (forbidden), and we, the People of the Household, do not seek cure with the forbidden (substances).'

key_terms.نَبِيذ: Nabidh (fermented drink, often from dates or raisins)

ai.seo_question: Why did Ismail ibn Ja'far consider Nabidh to be forbidden for his own medical treatment?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the medical prudence of Imam al-Sadiq (AS) by sending Ismail ibn Ja'far for examination, illustrating the practical application of fiqh in healthcare. Ismail’s declaration that the Ahl al-Bayt do not seek cure through haram substances establishes a key principle of 'purity of means,' distinguishing their medical practices from general permissibility of consuming wine for thirst or dissimulation (taqiyyah) as discussed in the chapter's title. This underscores the spiritual and physical integrity of the Imams, who avoid impurity even in healing.
